sam.name: Sam Park
sam.role: engineer (someone who designs and builds things to solve problems)

case.title: The Star Party Wish List
case.hook: Great news: the red tide is gone! To celebrate, Palmetto Beach is having a star party (a night of looking at the sky together). Four kids sent me wishes, but the town can rent just ONE tool.

notice.head: Palmetto Beach · Star Party Night
notice.title: Saturday, 8 PM, on the beach
rows: The town can rent ONE tool.
Pick what to bring so every kid gets their wish.

wishes.t: I want to see the craters on the Moon!
The Seven Sisters stars my grandma told me about.
The FARTHEST thing anybody has ever seen.

case.question: What should Sam bring so every wish comes true?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Things in space are so far away that their light is old. Andromeda’s light left it 2.5 million years ago.
Far things look dim. A bigger opening gathers more light. Zooming in alone doesn’t help.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: find it in the sky
clues.t: A backyard telescope shows Moon craters and Saturn’s rings. Binoculars fit the wide Seven Sisters.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: stare at nothing
clues.t: The farthest things need a space telescope. Webb stared at one “empty” speck for 12.5 hours and found thousands of galaxies.

solve.title: What should Sam bring?
solve.q: Which plan fits all four clues?

options.t: Rent a space telescope for the beach, so every wish comes true.
options.why: Check Clue 4. Where do space telescopes work? Could anyone bring one to a beach?

options.t: Just bring binoculars. They are easy to carry and show everything.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Can binoculars show Saturn’s rings?

options.t: Rent a backyard telescope for the Moon and Saturn. Bring binoculars for the Seven Sisters. Show Webb’s picture for the farthest thing.
options.why: Case cracked! The right tool for each wish. Now fill in Sam’s star party permit, just below.

racelight.afterText: Let’s race the light and find out
racelight.title: Race the light
todo: Guess first: drag each picture onto when you think its light left (or tap a card, then a spot).
Press Send the light. Watch each light race to you.

why.t: Light is the fastest thing there is, but space is huge. Light from far away has traveled a long time.

racelight.trayLabel: Drag each one onto your guess:

objs.name: The Moon
objs.alt: The full Moon, gray with dark patches

objs.name: Sirius, a bright star
objs.alt: The bright star Sirius, a white glow with light spikes

objs.name: The Andromeda Galaxy
objs.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a huge glowing oval of stars

racelight.q: Which light has been traveling the longest to reach you?

opts.miss: Look at your stamps. 8 minutes is not very long. Which one says millions?
The Moon is the closest. Its light takes about 1 second.

racelight.credit: Full Moon: NASA Goddard / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (public domain). The Sun: NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory (public domain). Sirius (the bright star) and its tiny partner star: NASA, ESA, H. Bond and M. Barstow, Hubble Space Telescope (public domain). The Andromeda Galaxy: Andy Weeks (CC0, no rights reserved). All via Wikimedia Commons. Palmetto Beach, the kids and the star party are made up for this lesson.
racelight.win: True! Starlight is old. The farther away something is, the longer its light travels, and the dimmer it looks. That’s a clue.

openwide.afterText: COLLECTS light from far away and focuses it
openwide.title: Open wider
todo: This is a model of the sky over Palmetto Beach. Drag the gold dot outward to open the light opening wider (or press Open wider).
Watch the star count. Then press Zoom only and compare.

why.t: Light gets into your eye through the pupil (the dark circle). A bigger opening catches more light, like a bigger bucket catches more rain.

stops.name: Your eye
stops.note: In the dark, your pupil opens to about 7 mm. Only the brightest stars send enough light.

stops.name: A barred owl
stops.alt: A barred owl with big, dark eyes
stops.note: Owls have huge eyes that let in more light, so they can hunt at night.

stops.name: Binoculars
stops.gain: About 50 times more light than your eye
stops.note: Each lens is about 50 mm wide. Many more stars pop out.

stops.name: Backyard telescope
stops.alt: A white backyard telescope on the grass, pointed at the sky
stops.gain: About 800 times more light than your eye
stops.note: Its mirror gathers about 800 times more light than your eye. Even a faint galaxy shows up.

openwide.zoomNote: Zoom made the stars bigger and dimmer, but no NEW stars appeared. Only a bigger opening gathers more light.
openwide.tryZoom: Now press Zoom only. Does zooming in show you any NEW stars?
openwide.q: What makes a telescope show MORE stars than your eye?

opts.t: Its big mirror gathers much more light.

opts.miss: Try Zoom only again. Bigger didn’t show any new stars, did it?

opts.t: It brings the stars closer to Earth.
opts.miss: The stars don’t move at all. What changed when you opened wider?

openwide.credit: Barred owl: Mara Koenig / U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (public domain). Backyard (Dobsonian) telescope: James Stewart (public domain). All via Wikimedia Commons. Palmetto Beach, the kids and the star party are made up for this lesson. The sky is a model drawn for this lesson, not a photo.
openwide.win: Far things look dim because only a little of their light reaches you. A bigger opening gathers more of it. That’s a clue.

skyhunt.afterText: Sam set up two tools on the beach
skyhunt.title: Find it in the sky
todo: Pick a tool. Then drag the circle across the sky (or tap a spot) to aim it.
Look at each one with BOTH tools. Then pick the best tool for it.

why.q: Why is the telescope circle so small?
why.t: A telescope zooms in a lot, so it sees a tiny piece of sky. Binoculars see a much wider piece.

skyhunt.emptyLine: Just dark sky. Move the circle onto something.

targets.name: The Moon

bino.note: The whole Moon fits. You can see dark patches and some big craters.

scope.note: Craters inside craters! The Moon is too big to fit all at once.

targets.q: Maya wants the Moon’s craters. Best tool?

opts.miss: Binoculars show some craters. Which tool showed craters inside craters?

targets.name: Seven Sisters

bino.note: The whole cluster fits. Your eyes see about 6 or 7 stars; binoculars show dozens.

scope.note: Too close! Only one or two stars fit in the tiny view.

targets.q: Ava wants the Seven Sisters. Best tool?

opts.miss: How many of the sisters fit in the telescope’s tiny view?

targets.name: Jupiter

bino.note: A tiny dot with up to four tiny moons in a line. (A drawing.)

scope.note: A round world with cloud stripes. (Real Hubble photo; a backyard view is smaller.)

targets.q: To see Jupiter’s cloud stripes, which tool?

opts.miss: Binoculars showed a dot. Where did you see stripes?

targets.name: Saturn

bino.note: A tiny yellow dot. No rings yet. (A drawing.)

scope.note: RINGS! At 100x or more they’re easy to see. (Real Hubble photo; a backyard view is smaller.)

targets.q: Leo wants Saturn’s rings. Best tool?

opts.miss: Look again with binoculars. Can you see any rings?

skyhunt.credit: Full Moon: NASA Goddard / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (public domain). The Seven Sisters star cluster (Pleiades): NASA, ESA, AURA/Caltech, Palomar Observatory (public domain). Jupiter: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (public domain). Saturn: NASA / Hubble Space Telescope, 2018 (public domain). All via Wikimedia Commons. Palmetto Beach, the kids and the star party are made up for this lesson. The sky, the dots and the binocular views of Jupiter and Saturn are drawings.
skyhunt.win: Binoculars show wide things, like a star cluster. A backyard telescope shows small, far details, like Saturn’s rings. That’s a clue.

tv.afterText: Sam found an old TV news report
tv.title: A telescope leaves Florida
todo: Press Watch the report. Turn on your sound.
tv.headline: HUBBLE SPACE TELESCOPE LAUNCHES

slides.alt: A space shuttle rises on a column of fire and smoke beside launch towers by the water.
slides.cap: Discovery lifts off from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, with Hubble inside. Another shuttle, Columbia, waits on the next pad.

slides.alt: A space shuttle climbing into a blue sky on a bright flame.
The Hubble Space Telescope, a silver tube with wing-like solar panels, floating above Earth.
slides.cap: Hubble in space, high above the air. (Photo from 2009.)

lines: This is a special report from Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
Moments ago, the space shuttle Discovery blasted off, carrying the Hubble Space Telescope.
Tomorrow, astronauts will set Hubble free, more than three hundred miles above Earth.
Up there, it will be above the blurry, wobbly air that makes stars twinkle.
Scientists say its giant mirror will see farther and sharper than any telescope on the ground.
tv.ticker: HUBBLE SPACE TELESCOPE · LAUNCHED APRIL 24, 1990 · KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, FLORIDA · MIRROR: ABOUT 8 FEET WIDE · ORBIT: MORE THAN 300 MILES UP ·
tv.q: Why did scientists put Hubble in space?

opts.t: To get above the blurry air
To get closer to the stars
opts.miss: Hubble is about 300 miles up. The stars are trillions of miles away. What did the report say about the air?

opts.t: Because it was too big for Florida
opts.miss: Listen again. What does the air do to starlight?

tv.credit: Discovery lifts off with Hubble, April 24, 1990: NASA (public domain). STS-31 liftoff: NASA (public domain). Hubble in orbit, 2009: NASA, STS-125 crew (public domain). All via Wikimedia Commons. Palmetto Beach, the kids and the star party are made up for this lesson. The report is read by a voice actor for this lesson.
tv.win: Right! Earth’s air blurs starlight and makes stars twinkle. Above the air, Hubble’s pictures are sharp.

deepfield.afterText: Jordan wants the farthest thing anyone has ever seen
deepfield.title: Stare at nothing
todo: Look at the tiny square of “empty” sky with each tool, in order.
With Webb, press and HOLD the shutter button until 12.5 hours have passed.

why.t: Hold a grain of sand at arm’s length. That’s how much sky this is, and it looks empty.

tools.note: Nothing. Just dark sky and a few stars around the speck.
Still nothing in the speck. It looks empty.
Two very faint, fuzzy smudges. Something is there, but it’s too dim to see.
Webb is a space telescope with a mirror about 21 feet wide. Press and hold to open its shutter.

hold.btn: Press and HOLD to open Webb’s shutter
hold.label: Shutter open
hold.letGo: You let go, so the shutter closed. Press and hold again to keep collecting light.

deepfield.doneNote: After 12.5 hours, almost every speck is a galaxy with billions of stars. Some of this light traveled over 13 billion years.
deepfield.alt: Webb’s First Deep Field: thousands of glowing galaxies on black, some round, some spiral, some stretched into curved arcs, and a few stars with long spikes.

shapes.found: A big round galaxy! It’s part of a giant group of galaxies.
A spiral galaxy, shaped like a pinwheel, like our own Milky Way.
A stretched, bent galaxy! Its light was bent on the way here by the giant group of galaxies in front of it.

star.t: That one is a star in our own galaxy, much closer. The long spikes give it away. Find a galaxy shape instead.

deepfield.hint: Look for a big round glow in the middle, a pinwheel on the right, and a curved streak near the top.
deepfield.lockLine: Look through the tool before this one first.
deepfield.q: Why could Webb see these galaxies when the backyard telescope couldn’t?

opts.t: Its huge mirror gathered light for hours, out in space.
It flew close to the galaxies.
opts.miss: Webb is about a million miles from Earth. These galaxies are billions of light-years away. What did it do for 12.5 hours?
Remember Open wider: zoom alone doesn’t show new things. What does Webb’s mirror gather?

deepfield.credit: Webb’s First Deep Field: NASA, ESA, CSA and STScI (public domain). All via Wikimedia Commons. Palmetto Beach, the kids and the star party are made up for this lesson. The views through your eyes, binoculars and the backyard telescope are drawings.
deepfield.win: The farthest things need the biggest light-gatherer, out in space, looking for a long time. That’s your last clue.

permit.title: The star party permit
todo: Tap the darkest place on this real photo of Florida at night. Then pick why.
permit.head: TOWN OF PALMETTO BEACH · EVENT PERMIT
rows: Backyard telescope (rented), binoculars, Webb’s deep field picture
permit.mapQ: Where are the stars easiest to see? Tap the darkest spot.
permit.alt: Florida at night from space: bright city lights along the coasts and around Orlando, and a big dark area in the south.

spots.miss: Miami is one of the brightest places in the photo. City lights hide faint stars.
Look at all those lights around Tampa Bay. Find a darker spot.
Orlando glows at night. Look south for a dark place.

spots.why: Big Cypress National Preserve is so dark that it is an official Dark Sky Park. Sam will take the star party bus there!

permit.whyQ: Why does a dark place help?

whyOpts.t: City lights wash out faint stars.
whyOpts.fill: Big Cypress is dark. City lights wash out faint stars.

whyOpts.miss: The stars are just as far away everywhere in Florida. What is different about the ground there?
Warm or cool, what makes stars hard to see? Look at the photo again.

permit.sign: Approved for Sam Park · Town of Palmetto Beach
permit.lockLine: Crack the case first. Then Sam’s permit opens.

ps.head: P.S. from Sam: telescopes look down, too!
ps.alt: Florida from space in daytime: green land, white clouds, and bright blue-green water swirling along the Gulf coast.
ps.t: A real NASA satellite photo of Florida from more than 400 miles up. Scientists watch the water’s color from space to spot blooms like red tide. On this day, most of the blue-green swirls were mud stirred up by a storm. That’s why scientists still take water samples, like we did!
ps.tease: See Florida from more than 400 miles up.
ps.credit: Florida’s coast from NASA’s Terra satellite (MODIS), Feb. 14, 2023: NASA (public domain). Via Wikimedia Commons.

permit.credit: Florida at night from the International Space Station, Oct. 13, 2014: NASA Johnson Space Center (public domain). Via Wikimedia Commons. Big Cypress National Preserve became an International Dark Sky Park in 2016.

q1.B: Bacteria are tiny and close. That’s a microscope’s job. What does a telescope collect?
q1.C: Close-up insects need a hand lens or microscope. What does a telescope do with far-away light?

q2.A: Saturn looks like a bright dot to your eyes. Which tool showed the rings in Find it in the sky?
q2.C: A hand lens is for close things. Saturn is about 900 million miles away!

q3.A: Space telescopes cost billions of dollars! What did the TV report say about the air?
q3.B: Telescopes collect light, not sound. What blurs the view from the ground?

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: Earth’s air blurs starlight. Hubble sits above the air, so its pictures are sharp.
Zooming in only made stars bigger and dimmer. It didn’t show any new stars.
Webb gathered light for 12.5 hours from space and found thousands of galaxies in an “empty” speck.
Even a tall telescope on Earth still looks up through the air.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · the star party
welcome.script: Great news! The red tide is gone, and Palmetto Beach is open again. So the town is throwing a star party, a night when everyone looks at the sky together. Four kids sent me their wish cards. Read them! The town can rent just one tool. Can we make every wish come true?

warmup.label: Warm-Up · race the light (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Here’s a wild claim: the starlight you see tonight is older than you. Let’s test it. Drag each picture onto your guess. How long ago did its light leave? Then press Send the light and watch it race to Earth.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Hold a paper towel tube to your eye for “telescope”; walk to the far side of the room for “distant”.

part1.label: Part 1 · open wider (Clue 2)
part1.script: Your eye is a light catcher. Drag the gold dot to open the opening wider. First an owl’s eye, then binoculars, then a telescope mirror. Watch the star count climb! Then try Zoom only. Do you see any new stars?

part2.label: Part 2 · find it in the sky (Clue 3)
part2.script: I set up two tools on the beach. Pick the binoculars or the telescope, then drag the circle across the sky. Look at every wish with both tools. The telescope sees more detail, but its view is tiny!

part3.label: Part 3 · the TV report
part3.notes: Optional video. The TV report itself is voiced by the news voice.

explore.label: Part 4 · stare at nothing (Clue 4)
explore.script: Jordan wants the farthest thing ever. Look at this tiny square of sky with each tool. Your eyes, binoculars, then the telescope. Then use Webb! Press and hold the shutter button. Keep holding until twelve and a half hours pass. Then tap three galaxy shapes.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab. Then fill in my star party permit and find the darkest place on the map. After that, answer two questions, write three views for Part C, and finish your C-E-R.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says we don’t need space telescopes. Just build them taller on Earth! Hmm. Think about the blurry air from the TV report. Think about Zoom only. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! Every kid gets their wish, because you picked the right tool for each one. Binoculars, a backyard telescope, and a space telescope. Next week my tools get a new job. How does energy make things move?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how tools help us see things too far away?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A telescope’s big mirror gathers much more light than your eye.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “big mirror”, “gathers” and “more light”. Those words tell how a telescope works. Small words like “a” and “than” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

constellation.name: TELESCOPIUM
constellation.meaning: means “the telescope.” It’s a real constellation!
constellation.note: A French astronomer named it in the 1750s. He also named Microscopium, the microscope!
constellation.hint: Each clue you find lights a star. Find all four and see what they draw.

starchart.kicker: Bonus · for a real night out
starchart.title: My star party sky chart

why.t: Yes! A computer worked out where the stars and Saturn are over Florida in mid-January at 8 PM. The lines show Orion, the hunter.

starchart.alt: A round chart of the night sky over Florida in mid-January at 8 PM, with Orion, Sirius, the Seven Sisters, Saturn and the North Star marked.
starchart.how: Hold the chart up over your head. Turn it until NORTH on the chart points north. When you look up, east really is on your left!
checks: Orion’s belt: three stars in a row
Sirius, the brightest star (its light left about 9 years ago!)
The Seven Sisters, almost straight up
Saturn: golden and steady, in the southwest
The North Star, low in the north
Bonus, from a dark place: the Andromeda Galaxy, a faint fuzzy smudge
starchart.note: The Moon moves every night, so it isn’t on the chart. Bright Jupiter rises in the east around 8 PM. Go out with a grown-up!
starchart.credit: Star and Saturn positions worked out for Orlando, Florida, on January 14, 2027, at 8 PM, with the PyEphem astronomy program. The chart is close for any night in mid-January and anywhere in Florida.
